body_markdown:
The garage serves many purposes for old car lovers. A sanctuary, storage unit, and a skunkworks all wrapped into one, the four walls and big door house objects of our affection and also our ideas and experiments. All that thinking and fiddling takes space, so organization is critical.


After years of working in my shop while accumulating more things I couldn’t live without and rarely letting things leave, it was time for a big reorganization to remind myself what I had and then to pack it back in tighter than ever. Here are five things I discovered during my garage shuffle.


## Overspray, everywhere


It’s not unusual for me to paint a small part standing right in the center of the shop.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Of all the bad habits that hadn’t caught up to me yet, painting parts in the middle of the garage might be the most subtly impactful in that it gets *everywhere* . I spray away without a care in the world where the rest of the paint goes, so long as the subject part gets nicely coated. After all, aerosol paint cans are a gift to DIYers like me and allow even professional-quality results without the need for compressors, booths, and mixing stations with inventory.


Those same cans also enable me to deposit paint on not just the part I’m hoping to, but also literally everything else in the shop. Oftentimes, overspray is nearly unnoticeable, but over time it adds up until the once so-smooth paint on a motorcycle gas tank or the visor on a helmet is suddenly not as smooth or as clear as they used to be. Luckily, a clay bar and some elbow grease with a light hand polish have been the solutions that erase the evidence of my own stupidity.


## Wire wheels are the devil


Not the best looking, but that’s a lot of stuff packed on shelves.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


While cleaning out this corner to replace the shelf, I found a lot of loose wheel wires.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


I’m not talking about the nice ones found on British cars or a certain era, but the ones that spin on a drill, bench grinder, or rotary tool. These little brushes have the magical ability to relatively delicately remove corrosion and paint while also depositing small sharp wires *all over the shop* . This wouldn’t be such a problem if it were not for the dozens of tires rolling around on any given week as things get driven, shuffled, or otherwise used.


While keeping the thinnest tires—those from the motorcycles—up on castered stands helps, the number of times I’ve pulled these little wires out of the soles of my shoes, boots, tires, shirt, or pant leg is infuriating. They also serve as an ironclad reminder to never use a wire wheel without safety glasses. I might have pulled those wires out of everything else, but thankfully not my cornea.


## Out of sight, out of mind is real


My shop is not huge at 24’x30′ with only 8′ ceilings, yet like all garages it has the magical gift of being able to make even large, heavy, annoying things disappear into a corner for *years.* Add in the shelving, which was set up to enable things like engines, transmissions, and differentials to roll into convenient hiding spots and it’s easy to see why so much of my stuff didn’t get touched for nearly five years.


## Past me had a lot of ideas—or no idea


Two spare Corvair engines for a car that has never run anything other than beautifully.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


This engine is locked solid, and I couldn’t even get the heads off.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Of the items I unearthed by this recent reshuffle, the biggest head-scratchers are the items that went into storage rather than the trash can. Surely I was thinking some combination of “I’ll get to that some day” and “it has value so I’m not going to throw it out.” Regardless, this reorganization prompted the question of whether there was even enough there to justify going to the scrap yard.


Some of the items I kept make no sense even when I try and think like the Kyle from ten years ago. While it was a great idea to hold onto everything to build a second powerpack for my 1965 Corvair, it was something that never got off the ground, and these days the parts would likely be better put to use by someone else doing a restoration or repairing a damaged car. Some things will definitely find new homes soon.


## It takes a lot of space to organize


There is a Corvette on jackstands in this photo.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


When everything is put away, this garage has plenty of space for me, yet all it takes is getting a new shelf for one of the walls to grind any vehicle projects to a halt. Just pulling most, not all, of the items I have stored in the garage out for a quick look before putting them back takes a surprising amount of time and space to accomplish. The ever-growing pile of things to get rid of by selling, scrapping, or giving away is at once exciting—I’m regaining space—but also sad, because I obviously kept some items for a reason and I never actually followed through on their potential. Oh well, can’t fix them all, and with any luck I can find the right home for some of these bits.


As everything starts to go back into place, I hope this reorganization period can be a positive launch into the long Michigan winter where the garage becomes the easiest escape. I’d like to enjoy the season working on projects in there rather than the garage itself, but at this rate my winter project might be building a couple of workbenches and trying different layouts until walking through the door feels like arriving at the hometown bar on Friday night. I guess I should restock the fridge before I get back to work.
